item.title: Three People Are Killed at a Minnesota Day Care Center
item.description:
Two adults and a child were killed Wednesday morning at a small day care center in a Minneapolis suburb, police officials said.

The three victims were members of a family, Brent Johnson, the police chief in Hopkins, Minn., told reporters. The assailant, a man, was among those who died, Chief Johnson said.

Chief Johnson called the attack a domestic situation and said investigators did not believe there was a continuing threat. The killings happened around 9 a.m., he said. Chief Johnson said that investigators believe that the two adults who died owned the day care, which operated inside their home.

Six other children who were at the in-home day care center were reunited with their parents, he said.

“This is a horrific, tragic situation for any community, especially here in Hopkins, where we don’t see this type of crime,” Chief Johnson said.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: How the Polls Got it So Wrong in Wisconsin
item.description:
For months, polls indicated that Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, was far and away the front-runner in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin.

Then David Crowley, a moderate and the chief executive of Milwaukee County, won the race, albeit narrowly.

The result comes just one week after Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, significantly underperformed polls to eke out a narrow victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary.

Why were the polls so wrong?

Possible explanations range from a genuine, last-minute change in voter sentiment — Ms. Hong, a state representative, faced significant negative publicity in the closing days of the race — to miscalculations by pollsters about the makeup of the primary electorate.

The disparity between polls and results in Wisconsin and Michigan prompted Frank Luntz, a Republican pollster and consultant, to jokingly call for “a total and complete shutdown of primary polling in the Midwestern United States until we can figure out what the hell is going on” in an early-morning X post on Wednesday.

The Wisconsin primary drew a crowded field of candidates after Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, announced last summer that he would not seek re-election. Here’s what experts, pollsters and the data say about the results of the Democratic primary to replace him:

The Wisconsin governor’s race was tumultuous. Mr. Crowley had suspended his campaign just over a month ago after polls indicated he had failed to gain traction. Then he re-entered the contest and won.

“The polls were made out of date very quickly” as a result, said Celinda Lake, a Democratic pollster from Michigan.

In a survey taken by Marquette Law School just after Mr. Crowley re-entered the race in mid-July, 38 percent of respondents said they favored Ms. Hong. Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor, was in second place at 16 percent, and Mr. Crowley had just 7 percent of the vote.

But almost as large as Ms. Hong’s vote share was the percentage of undecided survey respondents: 34 percent.

Mr. Barnes dropped out after that poll was released.

In the weeks that followed, surveys continued to show voter support was fractured among Ms. Hong’s numerous opponents.

As recently as last week, a poll conducted by Mr. Crowley’s campaign found him trailing Ms. Hong by 18 percentage points. He trailed Ms. Hong by 22 points in another poll from State Navigate, which surveys in state-level elections.

Polls failed to predict the outcome of Tuesday’s election, but they did not significantly overestimate Ms. Hong’s portion of the vote. Most surveys estimated she would win about 40 percent of the vote, and she ended up winning 39 percent.

What changed was Mr. Crowley’s support. In a ballot-counting marathon that stretched into the wee hours of Wednesday morning, he over-performed the Marquette poll’s estimate by more than 30 points.

In the end, Mr. Crowley was less than half of a percentage point — or just under 4,000 votes — ahead of Ms. Hong on Wednesday morning, with more than 95 percent of ballots counted.

Mr. Crowley may owe much of his success to the support of previously undecided voters.

In primaries, news coverage and campaign advertising tend to increase in the last weeks of the race. And voters may not research candidates until minutes before they walk into the voting booth. In some Wisconsin polls, as many as one-third of voters said they were undecided heading into Election Day.

“It is well known that voters in Wisconsin tend to make up their minds, tend to start paying attention to primary elections pretty late in the game,” said Anthony Chergosky, an associate professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse.

Ms. Hong faced a barrage of negative press in the election’s final days, after six-year-old social media posts surfaced in which she called to defund and abolish the police and “cancel Thanksgiving.”

Mr. Crowley was not as well-known to voters before he re-entered the race in July. Mr. Evers campaigned energetically for him, and a super PAC supporting him also spent heavily on ads disparaging Ms. Hong in recent weeks.

The governor’s late endorsement made the race unusual, said Charles Franklin, who conducts the Marquette University Law School poll.

“In our final poll, 36 percent of Democratic primary voters said that endorsement made them more likely to support Crowley,” said Mr. Franklin. “Evers’s job approval with Democrats was also over 85 percent.”

Mr. Crowley may also have consolidated support from moderates after the early establishment-backed candidate, Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, and Mr. Barnes ended their campaigns last month.

Even after an internal poll found that Mr. Crowley was trailing Ms. Hong last week, his campaign manager predicted that polls would not reflect the primary results.

In a memo to supporters on Aug. 5 obtained by The New York Times, the campaign manager, Garren Randolph, argued that Wisconsin surveys overrepresented voters between the ages of 18 and 45. In some cases, polls expected twice as many young voters as actually showed up to vote in 2018 and 2022. Ms. Hong was strongest among young voters, according to the internal poll.

Across elections, primary voters tend to be older, and Wisconsin is no exception. Older voters and moderates were also more likely to remain undecided until close to the end, Mr. Franklin said, based on his polling data.

Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of the firm State Navigate, which conducted polls in Wisconsin, suggested that Ms. Hong’s early and enthusiastic supporters may simply have been more willing to respond to polls, thus skewing the results.

“One candidate’s supporters were just more eager to answer the poll,” Mr. Nuttycombe said.

Pollsters have long grappled with what is known as nonresponse bias, where certain voters may be more likely — or less likely — to respond to a poll.

The same issue may have occurred in Michigan. In a post-mortem of that state’s Democratic Senate primary, Adam Carlson, a Democratic pollster, speculated that the “main driving factor” behind the polling miss was selective responsiveness of voters.

“El-Sayed’s supporters were more fired up and willing to take polls down the stretch, but more enthusiasm does not necessarily equal more votes,” Mr. Carlson, the founding partner of Zenith Research, wrote in a post-mortem analysis on Monday.

Conducting surveys in partisan primaries has long been a challenge for pollsters, requiring them to make assumptions about the partisan composition of who will actually turn out to vote.

That is particularly difficult in states like Wisconsin and Michigan that hold open primaries and where voters are not registered by party.

As pollsters attempt to target likely Democratic primary voters in surveys, they are often unsure about the percentage of Republicans and independents who might vote in a given election.

Mr. Nuttycombe said polls likely underestimated the Republican share of the electorate.

“If Republicans did vote, they went overwhelmingly anti-Hong,” he said.

Mr. Carlson noted that in the Michigan Senate primary his likely voter model — which pollsters use to estimate who will actually vote in an election — probably underrepresented seniors, low-income Michiganders and self-identified Republicans.

Julie Bosman contributed reporting.

For me, one of the biggest takeaways here is that a significant number of Wisconsin voters— more than one-third in this case— remained undecided until the last weeks of the primary. It's a good reminder to pay attention to the "undecided" numbers in polls, rather than just the head-to-head comparisons between candidates, and a lesson about how voters make their decisions.

item.title: How Crowley Eked Out a Win in the Wisconsin Governor Primary
item.description:
Miriam Shelef, a physician in Madison, Wis., had a hunch that the polls were off.

Two weekends ago, after researching the candidates in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor, she began canvassing for David Crowley, whose record as the Milwaukee County executive impressed her.

At one house after another in her west side neighborhood, people changed their minds on the spot about supporting other candidates after hearing Dr. Shelef talk about Mr. Crowley’s perceived electability and his work on housing and cutting carbon emissions. One woman gave Dr. Shelef a warm hug, grabbed a Crowley sign and plunked it in her yard.

“I was like, oh my gosh, I think there’s clearly late enthusiasm for him,” Dr. Shelef said. “I was amazed at how popular Crowley was at the doors.”

On Wednesday morning, Wisconsin Democrats woke up to an unexpected result, as Mr. Crowley, a moderate who had briefly dropped out of the race, narrowly beat Francesca Hong, a chef and democratic socialist who had led in the polls for months.

With 95 percent of the votes counted, Mr. Crowley edged out Ms. Hong by fewer than 4,000 votes to the relief of the Wisconsin Democratic establishment, which had feared that Ms. Hong would lose in a November matchup with Representative Tom Tiffany, a Republican endorsed by President Trump.

Mr. Crowley’s 11th-hour surge may have been buoyed by the race’s rapid shifts in its final days, according to interviews with campaign officials, volunteers and voters. Mr. Crowley benefited from Ms. Hong’s missteps on social media and in national TV interviews as she backtracked from comments about hating Thanksgiving and abolishing the police.

He toured the state with Gov. Tony Evers, a popular leader who pulled Mr. Crowley back into the race after he abandoned his campaign last month and endorsed him. Perhaps most crucially, Mr. Crowley captured the notice of a large number of voters who had missed many of the primary’s earlier twists and remained undecided near the end.

In an interview, Mr. Crowley said that traveling with Mr. Evers showed voters that he could “coalesce people across the political spectrum to build the type of coalition needed to win,” he said. “That’s what we’re able to do, and I think that’s how we won this race.”

Election results showed that Mr. Crowley was popular across Wisconsin. He easily beat the other candidates in the Milwaukee region, won a large number of rural counties and even captured 37 percent of the vote to Ms. Hong’s 44 percent in Dane County, a liberal stronghold that was her physical and philosophical home base.

Many voters said they had tuned into the primary only in the last week, missing what had been a bumpy and dramatic campaign throughout the year. When they started paying attention, they said, Mr. Evers’s endorsement helped them decide.

One Crowley voter, Pam McAllister, a 72-year-old retired pharmacist in Verona, Wis., said on Tuesday that she disliked Ms. Hong’s politics. Her second-most important reason for voting for Mr. Crowley: “Because Evers endorsed him.”

“Evers’s endorsement gave Crowley attention and voters the encouragement to give Crowley a look,” said Alex Lasry, a prominent Democrat in Wisconsin who supported Mr. Crowley. “Once they did, they saw Crowley was not only part of the next generation of leaders, but also very experienced and the right person to lead Wisconsin forward.”

After touring the state with Mr. Crowley for days, Mr. Evers appeared last weekend to be either resigned or confident. On Saturday night, he headed to a theater in rural Spring Green for some Shakespeare under the stars.

At one point in a soliloquy during “The Two Gentlemen of Verona,” an actor made a knowing reference to the perfect lover having little to say — and looked directly to the front row at Mr. Evers, who is not known for his loquaciousness. The audience burst into laughter.

On Wednesday morning, after Mr. Tiffany’s overwhelming primary victory, Republicans hinted that they would frame the general election campaign as a battle against leftist extremism despite Mr. Crowley’s moderate credentials.

“Democrats are moving further and further to the left,” Brian Schimming, the chairman of WisGOP, said in a statement. “This election comes down to the difference between common sense and radicalism.”

Mr. Crowley’s first stop on Wednesday was in Milwaukee, where he was mobbed with hugs from supporters and, in his remarks, promised to leave behind the divisive Democratic primary and focus on Mr. Tiffany.

One Crowley supporter in attendance, Stephanie Johnson, said that she had been drawn to his campaign because of his work for low-income people in Milwaukee, especially the homeless. “You hear everybody talk about the working class, but what about the ones at the bottom?” she said.

Mr. Crowley specifically thanked Ms. Hong, saying that her campaign “reminded people across Wisconsin that there are no long shots when it comes to believing in a better future and fighting to expand opportunity for every family.” They later had breakfast with other Democrats in Madison before television cameras, sharing a meal intended to show unity for the campaign ahead.

item.title: With Big Choices Ahead, Ocasio-Cortez Navigates New Territory
item.description:
Since she won her first election in 2018 at 28, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, has been a political obsession for fans to adore and critics to abhor.

Her body, her weight, the clothes she wore in magazine shoots, her lipstick, her endorsements, her ill-fated decision to attend the Met Gala in a “tax the rich” gown, have been parsed and picked apart, in ways she has described as sometimes “dehumanizing” even when that parsing was coming from her supporters.

One area where she was insulated from such scrutiny was her love life: Ms. Ocasio-Cortez arrived on the national political scene with her boyfriend from college, Riley Roberts, by her side. And he stayed there as she became one of the most consequential women in American politics, a burly redhead who stood mostly outside the frame of Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s public life. In 2022, her team announced in a fund-raising email that the couple was engaged.

Four years later, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is at a new juncture. Her relationship with Mr. Roberts quietly ended some time ago and her decision to livestream her egg-freezing journey has forced to the forefront an uncomfortable topic for a lawmaker who is both unusually open and incredibly private: a breakup that she had never broadcast, despite giving her followers a sense that they are often along with her for the ride.

The new information about Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s private life is coming alongside a spate of speculation that she’s preparing to run for president. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who has said she hasn’t ruled out a presidential run or a run for Senate, could now be navigating a possible national or statewide campaign as a young, world-famous, single woman, a profile that would only intensify the ideological and cultural debates that swirl around her.

The reality of that new level of exposure became apparent on Tuesday night after a reporter for Puck and TMZ reported that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had split with Mr. Roberts, which was confirmed to The New York Times by multiple people knowledgeable about her personal life. Her relationship status was not new, but public disclosure of it all but broke the internet.

“All the single left-wing men in this city are about to line up nightly for dinner in her district until she picks one like the suitors in The Odyssey,” Asad Dandia, a Brooklyn-based community organizer, wrote on X.

As early as 2020, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was open about struggling to find a balance between life and work. “I’m sitting here, I’m like, Do I freeze my eggs? Can I afford to do that?” she asked in an interview with Vanity Fair that year. “My orthodontist was telling me about how she was doing I.V.F., and I’m, like, asking her what her experience is like.”

Diana Z. O’Brien, chair of women, gender and sexuality studies at Washington University in St. Louis, said that as a 36-year-old progressive lightning rod with political ambitions outside of the House, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had no real choice but to make public her decision to freeze her eggs — and then, by association, her breakup.

“If she says nothing, then people will infer that she’s making a decision to de-prioritize family,” Ms. O’Brien said.

Ms. O’Brien said it was inevitable that with that disclosure came the less comfortable one, about her relationship status.

“It came up for Senator Cory Booker before he was married, so it will definitely come up for a woman,” she said. “This allows her to say, ‘yes, I’m single right now, but that doesn’t mean I intend to be child-free or single forever.’ It counterbalances a narrative that would try to portray her as a very particular type of leftist single woman who hates men.”

David Axelrod, the former top adviser to President Barack Obama, said that being an unmarried woman “probably adds a degree of difficulty” to any run she might make to become the first woman elected president, although he noted that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez operates in her own orbit and according to her own rules because of her “unique ability to take people along for the ride in a way that is personally connecting.”

He added: “The bigger question to me is whether this is a ride she wants or needs to take at this stage because it would require an absolute surrender of so much of her life.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has not publicly addressed the end of her relationship, but that has not stopped anyone from weighing in on it. Conservatives piled on to criticize her for putting her political ambitions above her relationship. And group chats lit up with ideas for who Ms. Ocasio-Cortez might date without their politics being picked apart: A chef? A musician? A Knick?

On Capitol Hill, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s colleagues have long known she was no longer engaged. And she has not exactly hidden it. For one thing, she doesn’t wear an engagement ring. But she has also not gone public about her relationship status or whether she is dating again.

When a reporter asked her on Sunday what her fiancé thought of her decision to freeze her eggs, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez sidestepped the question, noting only that “all of my loved ones have been very supportive.” Her chief of staff, Mike Casca, did not respond to a request for comment for this piece.

But the reality is that being a prominent young, single woman lawmaker draws attention and poses challenges that men with a similar profile might not encounter, including reproductive choices.

Representative Yassamin Ansari, the 34-year-old Democrat from Arizona, said dating can be difficult when she feels like she is never in one place for long.

“I have my Arizona life and I have my D.C. life and I never feel like I’m rooted somewhere,” she said in an interview. Ms. Ansari said she was in a relationship when she was first elected in 2024, but that it ended in part because “it was super difficult for me to prioritize that on top of everything else going on.” As for dating, she said she prefers meeting people in real life and that “the apps do make me nervous. The job responsibilities make everything more challenging.”

She added: “I will probably freeze my eggs, too.”

For Ms. Ocasio-Cortez the scrutiny exists at another level. Over the years, she has given her followers a sense of shared intimacy by allowing them to watch her make black bean soup and assemble IKEA furniture on social media while talking about policy and answering questions about her daily routines. She participated in an emotional livestream after the Jan. 6 mob attack on the Capitol, describing in detail the trauma she felt from the day.

But being vulnerable and prominent has not been without cost, or easy.

“I miss being able to go outside in sweats,” she told Time magazine in 2019, just after she was elected. “I can’t go anywhere in public and just be a person without a lot of people watching everything I do.”

After she was criticized for attending the Met Gala, despite her Democratic Socialist politics, she wrote online: “I and my body have been so heavily and relentlessly policed from all corners politically since the moment I won my election.”

Jessica Valenti, the feminist writer who publishes the popular newsletter, “Abortion, Every Day,” said that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was so triggering to the right because she represents a direct affront to their well-funded message that women should get married young and have children young.

“Here, you have this very beautiful, very powerful woman, who is creating the life that she wants and appears to be very happy,” she said. “A very big part of the conservative Republican agenda right now is targeting young women. The last thing they need is a young woman modeling what a life could look like that they are so desperate to stop.”

Ms. Valenti said that “to a certain group of people, there is nothing A.O.C. could ever do, nothing would be OK with them” and that will likely carry into her personal life. “Regardless of who she dates,” she said, “how public she is or how private she is, someone is going to have an issue with it.”

Indeed, Allie Beth Stuckey, a conservative commentator, wrote online that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was “glamorizing the lie that women can have it all. You can’t. Biology is real and how you order your life makes or breaks your future.” Ms. Stuckey’s criticism was emblematic of the view from the Christian right on reproductive rights like egg-freezing and I.V.F., which remains culturally contested ground when it comes to judging the personal choices of a young lawmaker.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has long been self-aware about the strangeness of growing up in a political petri dish. In her livestream on Sunday, she told her followers that the downside of being elected as a young person is “you have to then grow up in the public eye in a time that most people get to grow more privately.”

She added: “when you get elected later in life, you’ve made all of your mistakes in private. When you get elected when you’re young, you have to do all of that in public.”

As she prepared to inject her exposed belly with a fertility shot, she warned viewers, “don’t be weird about this,” no doubt knowing full well that they almost certainly would be.

item.title: Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s Press Secretary, to Depart White House
item.description:
Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary and one of the most public-facing officials in the Trump administration, will step down to spend more time with her family, she and President Trump announced on Wednesday.

In a social media post, Mr. Trump said that Ms. Leavitt, who recently returned from maternity leave after giving birth to her second child, would leave at the end of the month to spend time with her young children — a decision that he said “I totally understand and respect.”

He said Ms. Leavitt would become one of his “top” outside advisers and called her “one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office.”

Ms. Leavitt’s departure comes at a critical time for the White House, as Mr. Trump faces multiple headwinds, foreign and domestic, and the midterm elections in November, in which he will need to sell policies that Ms. Leavitt was among the most effective at defending.

Mr. Trump said Ms. Leavitt would remain “an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.” He did not name a replacement in his announcement, nor a timeline for naming one.

Ms. Leavitt, 28, the youngest person to assume the role, worked for Mr. Trump in his first term and on his campaign. She said in a post on social media announcing her departure that serving as press secretary over the past year and a half had “been the honor and adventure of a lifetime.”

“Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least,” Ms. Leavitt continued.

“The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.”

She added that she would “always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party,” and that she would remain on the front lines of the party’s fight against what she called an “existential threat” by Democrats.

“My fight is entering a new phase,” she added, “but it is far from over.”

Mr. Trump cycled through four press secretaries during his first four years in office, and Ms. Leavitt was particularly adept at managing Mr. Trump’s expectations.

After working in the White House as an assistant press secretary and in the Office of Presidential Correspondence during the first Trump administration, Ms. Leavitt ran for Congress in New Hampshire in 2022, winning a Republican primary but failing to unseat a Democratic incumbent. She was also a spokeswoman for Representative Elise Stefanik of New York.

Ms. Leavitt quickly ascended to become one of Mr. Trump’s most loyal allies and fiercest defenders, making a steely debut in January 2025 at the age of 27.

Ms. Leavitt often expressed disdain for mainstream media. She regularly attacked unflattering coverage of Mr. Trump’s policies and often echoed the president’s falsehoods, mirroring his combative style with journalists.

In the briefing room, she fielded rapid-fire questions with information straight from the president’s mouth. She was also a regular in the media stratosphere, particularly conservative television, where she spoke regularly and directly to the American public.

Mr. Trump often gushed about Ms. Leavitt’s job performance, remarking on how her lips “move like a machine gun,” and once vowing that she would “never” be replaced. Mr. Trump proudly looked on last November after he summoned Ms. Leavitt to defend him as he took questions from reporters at a meeting with the Hungarian prime minister at the time, Viktor Orban. After Ms. Leavitt admonished reporters, Mr. Trump boasted that the autocratic leader asked if he could hire her.

Since returning to work in mid-July, Ms. Leavitt has been less of a fixture in the briefing room as she had been before she went on maternity leave in April and welcomed her second child, a girl, in May. During her maternity leave, the briefings dwindled after a spate of high-profile stand-ins, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

When she returned to the lectern in July, Ms. Leavitt kicked off her remarks by saying, “Let’s get back to work.”

Her first question was about how she managed to juggle her high-demanding jobs of working for the president and raising two children.

“I don’t think there is a secret,” she said. “You just have to show up every day and keep going.”

item.title: Two Killed in Military Helicopter Crash Near Fort Hood in Texas
item.description:
Two people died in a military helicopter crash on Wednesday outside Fort Hood in Texas, the authorities said.

The Bell County Sheriff’s Office received a 911 call just after 1:30 p.m. about a helicopter crash in Salado, a small town about 20 miles southeast of Fort Hood, a United States Army base.

The two people were pronounced dead around 2:30 p.m. local time, said Cliff Coleman, a spokesman for the sheriff’s office. He directed questions about the identity of the two people to the military.

“You could tell it was a violent crash,” Mr. Coleman said.

Officials at Fort Hood did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a news release, U.S. Army officials said the aircraft involved in the crash, an AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, was based at Fort Hood.

The crash caused a blaze in the dry fields where it landed and law enforcement officials evacuated several area residents, Mr. Coleman said.

The fire was not immediately contained, he said.

A number of military helicopters have crashed in Texas in recent decades. In 2015, four soldiers died when a Black Hawk helicopter crashed about 60 miles north of Austin. In 2004, a brigadier general and six soldiers in Texarkana, Texas, also aboard a Black Hawk, crashed into a transmission tower and died.

item.title: Treasury Scales Back Scrutiny of U.S. Shell Companies
item.description:
The Trump administration is moving forward with a plan to scale back scrutiny of the shadowy shell companies that criminals use to launder money and traffic drugs.

The initiative follows a yearslong campaign by lobbying groups, which contended that new financial reporting requirements were too onerous for businesses.

The Treasury Department said late on Tuesday that it was permanently halting the collection of data about the ownership of private American companies that was required as part of the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act. The law, which passed with bipartisan support, was intended to prevent the illicit use of shell companies by giving law enforcement agencies access to information about their ownership structures.

“Treasury is eliminating a burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a post on social media.

The law applied to a broad swath of private American businesses; however, there has been particular concern in the United States about shell companies. These are legal entities that do not usually have physical operations or assets and can be used for holding — and often hiding — financial assets in anonymous accounts.

The announcement finalized a temporary halt to collection of the data about “beneficial owners” that the Treasury Department put in place last year. Foreign companies are still required to report information about foreign owners to the department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, also known as FinCEN.

The decision raised questions about whether the Trump administration was essentially declining to carry out a law passed by Congress. It also appeared to undercut President Trump’s publicly stated ambitions of cracking down on financial crime, money laundering and drug trafficking.

“This is a gift to cartels, criminals and U.S. adversaries that exploit shell companies to move millions through our financial system,” said Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee. “The Trump administration has dismissed law enforcement warnings, ignored the role that shell companies play in crimes ranging from drug trafficking to fraud to sanctions evasion.”

The legislation was enacted in 2021 as part of a military spending bill. The backing of the bill, which was co-sponsored by Marco Rubio, then a Republican senator from Florida, was so strong that lawmakers overrode a presidential veto toward the end of Mr. Trump’s first term.

At the time, Mr. Rubio, who is now Mr. Trump’s secretary of state, called the legislation the “most significant anti-corruption and money laundering law in decades.”

Under the Corporate Transparency Act, beneficial owners are defined as shareholders who own 25 percent or more of a reporting company. They are also defined as individuals with “substantial control,” such as decision-making power, over a business.

According to the law, beneficial owners were supposed to submit their names, addresses, birth dates and up-to-date identification records — like a passport or a driver’s license — as part of their filing. Their information would later be shared with banks and law enforcement.

Small-business groups led a lobbying effort to compel the Treasury Department to water down and delay implementation of the law during the Biden administration. They maintained that the rules would be an expensive compliance burden.

“FinCEN’s final rule is a major victory for American small-business owners and financial privacy,” said Representative Warren Davidson, Republican of Ohio. “The Corporate Transparency Act buried millions of small-business owners, sole proprietors and even volunteer HOA leaders in costly reporting requirements while doing little to catch the criminals it was supposed to target.” Mr. Davidson was referring to homeowners associations.

The weakening of the law comes as the Trump administration has prioritized domestic investigations into money laundering, particularly in states led by Democrats. Earlier this year, Mr. Bessent unveiled an initiative to root out fraud and the misuse and potential laundering of federal funds in Minnesota. The Treasury Department has also expressed concern about the use of shell companies around the world as tools for evading sanctions.

Andrea Gacki, who resigned last month after serving for three years as director of FinCEN, had been a major proponent of the merits of the Corporate Transparency Act.

In a 2024 speech, she pointed to shell companies that were involved in crimes, including a Chicago flooring contractor that rigged bids and fixed prices, as well as the Sinaloa drug cartel’s $16.5 million transnational money laundering operation. She also made the case that beneficial ownership information could have made it easier for Treasury Department investigators to track the funds of Russian oligarchs who use shell companies to illegally hide assets in the United States.

“Beneficial ownership information reporting can make these types of investigations more efficient by providing a direct resource for law enforcement, national security and intelligence officials,” Ms. Gacki said. “It can give law enforcement an advantage over illicit actors, diminish the head start that corporate anonymity provides and ultimately level the playing field for legitimate American businesses.”

It is not clear that Mr. Bessent needed to curtail the law so dramatically to make it workable for businesses.

Alex Zerden, the founder of the risk advisory firm Capitol Peak Strategies and a former official in the Treasury Department’s Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, said the law provided leeway for the department to create exemptions to make compliance easier for small businesses.

“This is an example of throwing the baby out with the bath water,” Mr. Zerden said.

item.title: Johanna Fernández, Historian of the Young Lords, Dies at 55
item.description:
Johanna Fernández, a Dominican American historian whose authoritative book about the Young Lords helped revive the legacy of that leftist collective, a revolutionary Latino counterpart to the Black Panthers, died on July 30 in Manhattan. She was 55.

Her death, in a hospital, was caused by non-small-cell lung cancer, her brother Tirso Fernández Jr. said.

An associate professor of history at Baruch College, Dr. Fernández was unaware of the Young Lords until her junior year at Brown, when she took a class that covered the radical group and was angered that it had been effectively erased from public memory.

“I’d say that the children of migrants — especially from Latin America — connect more than anyone else with the history of the Young Lords,” she said in a 2020 interview with CounterPunch, a left-leaning website. “Because you wake up and all you see is death and abandoned buildings and you start believing what people and the media say about you.”

She added, “Then to see your own people take it and shred it and fight it in the streets — that’s freedom on a profound personal level.”

The Young Lords started as a street gang in Chicago and expanded to New York City in 1969. They were a confrontational, anticapitalist collective of Hispanic — mostly Puerto Rican — and Black activists who sought solutions to the deplorable conditions of neighborhoods like the South Bronx and Spanish Harlem.

To protest poor trash collection, they built walls of garbage across city streets, then set the walls on fire. They commandeered a church and used it to offer free breakfast to schoolchildren. They occupied a building at the dilapidated Lincoln Hospital in the Bronx, placed a Puerto Rican flag on the roof and made demands that included building a new hospital, door-to-door preventive care and opening a day care center for the children of patients and employees.

The group’s history was the subject of Dr. Fernández’s Ph.D. dissertation at Columbia, which she completed in 2004 and later expanded into a book.

“She interviewed me three times over 15 years,” the journalist Juan González, a founder of the group’s New York branch, said in an interview. “At first, she didn’t know a lot, but she was determined to speak to everyone. She spoke to a lot of people who weren’t speaking to each other because of past conflicts.”

Her research was impeded by the supposed inaccessibility of extensive surveillance files, more than 500 boxes’ worth, that had been accumulated by the New York Police Department’s secretive special services division from 1954 to 1972. She was told the files were missing or lost.

In 2014, after her Freedom of Information Law requests yielded little, she filed a lawsuit against the N.Y.P.D. seeking the documents. The suit was dismissed but, in 2016, a significant portion of the records of the department’s scrutiny of the Young Lords, the Black Panthers and the Nation of Islam resurfaced during an inventory of a Queens warehouse.

The files told the story of “thousands of people and organizations in New York City who fought to make the city more just and democratic and were systematically obstructed by the police,” Dr. Fernández said in a 2016 interview with The New York Times.

She used information gleaned from the files in her book “The Young Lords: A Radical History” (2020).

In his review in The Nation, Ed Morales, an expert on Latino politics, wrote that the book placed the Young Lords “in the context of the political and social debates that shaped the era and reveals how so much of their activism centered on the same issues — housing, health, education and the marginalization of women, the L.G.B.T.Q. community and the working poor — that we face today.”

“The Young Lords” won the 2021 Frederick Jackson Turner Award from the Organization of American Historians.

Johanna Luisa del Carmen Fernández was born in Manhattan on Dec. 2, 1970, and grew up in the Bronx. She was one of four children of Tirso Sr. and Minerva (Estevez) Fernández, immigrants from the Dominican Republic. Mr. Fernández was a maintenance worker, and Mrs. Fernández managed the home.

Dr. Fernández’s brother Tirso Jr. said their father “had been orphaned as a child and knew real hunger, but it didn’t harden him. Instead, it made him deeply compassionate.”

“Johanna took that and ran with it,” he added. “Her own intellect took her the rest of the way, into history, race, class, power.”

In addition to Tirso Jr., she is survived by her mother and two other brothers, Osvaldo and Geovanny.

In 1992, while attending Brown on an academic scholarship, Dr. Fernández was one of 253 students arrested for taking over an administration building; their demands included a need-blind admission policy. At one point, she attracted a crowd by delivering a speech from the open window of a bathroom. Need-blind admissions at Brown did not start until 2003.

She graduated in 1992 with a bachelor’s degree in English and American civilization, then earned an M.A. in 1996, an M.Phil. in 1999 and a Ph.D. in 2004, all in history from Columbia.

As a postdoctoral fellow at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh from 2005 to 2006, she grew interested in prison abolition and the case of Mumia Abu-Jamal, a former Black Panther and radio journalist then on death row after being convicted of murdering a white police officer in Philadelphia in 1981. To his supporters, Mr. Abu-Jamal is a political prisoner who should be released. To his critics, he is a celebrity cop killer.

Dr. Fernández told CounterPunch that visiting Mr. Abu-Jamal and other men on death row “transformed me, because you get a sense of a whole country of human beings who’ve been thrown away.”

She became close to Mr. Abu-Jamal. She wrote and produced “Justice on Trial: The Case of Mumia Abu-Jamal” (2010), a documentary about his case; edited a book of his prison writings that was published in 2015; and brought a trove of his papers to a permanent archive at Brown in 2024.

In 2012, a year after Mr. Abu-Jamal left death row — he is now serving a life sentence without the possibility of parole — Dr. Fernández began storing boxes of his materials in her apartment. “They were pressuring him to get rid of everything in his cell,” she told The Times. “He wanted to throw it all away. But as a historian, I understood the importance of papers.”

Mr. Abu-Jamal spoke by phone at Dr. Fernández’s funeral on Sunday, calling her “a shock of light in the darkness of death row,” according to her brother.

In 2015, she was a curator of “¡Presente! The Young Lords in New York,” an exhibition that was presented at El Museo del Barrio, the Bronx Museum and the Loisaida Inc. community center and showed the group as a cultural and political force.

An exhibition about the Latino civil rights movement of the 1960s — which Dr. Fernández organized with Felipe Hinojosa of Baylor University — was scheduled to open last year in Washington under the auspices of the Smithsonian Institution. But it was shelved after conservative commentators and members of Congress criticized a previous Smithsonian show about Latino history as Marxist.

With a grant from the Mellon Foundation, the project was revived in June at the Shed in Manhattan as an outdoor exhibition called “Latinx Freedom” that will be on display through Aug. 16 before touring to several American cities.

“She was such a joy — a relentless hard worker who was never satisfied with one answer,” Dr. Hinojosa said in an interview. “She took great offense at the kind of anti-Latino sentiment that exists in this country and worked as hard as she could to make people understand the gifts that Latinos bring to the United States.”

item.title: Mike Fincke, Astronaut Who Spent 549 Days in Space, Has Retired
item.description:
NASA announced the retirement on Wednesday of Michael Fincke, an astronaut who spent a total of 549 days in space, making him the astronaut with the fourth most time there in the space agency’s history. He also became the first person to ever need an evacuation from the International Space Station, the result of a medical situation.

During his 30-year career with the agency, Mr. Fincke, 59, served as a commander, mission specialist and flight engineer on his four missions to the space station, in addition to chief handyman.

“Few people have had the opportunity to shape as many chapters of NASA’s history as Mike Fincke,” NASA’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, said in a news release on Wednesday.

Mr. Fincke said he would “carry those lessons forward and help prepare the next generation of engineers, explorers and leaders.”

“NASA gave me the extraordinary privilege of serving alongside remarkable people, flying and helping develop spacecraft, and contributing to the International Space Station from its earliest days through command in orbit,” he said in a statement.

Starting in August 2025, Mr. Fincke served as pilot on NASA’s Crew‑11 mission to the space station, which launched in a SpaceX Dragon vehicle and returned to Earth in January.

That mission ended one month early because of a medical episode involving Mr. Fincke.

Five months into his stay, on Jan. 7, Mr. Fincke said he was eating dinner when he suddenly couldn’t talk. The episode lasted about 20 minutes, he said. Neither NASA nor Mr. Fincke has disclosed what caused the episode. But testing ruled out a heart attack or stroke, he said.

While Mr. Fincke’s condition was stable, NASA officials decided the safest course was to evacuate Mr. Fincke and his three crewmates back to Earth, leaving the space station with only three astronauts aboard rather than the typical complement of seven. It was the first time that astronauts were forced to return early because of a medical issue in the more than 25-year history of the space station.

Mr. Fincke is a native of Emsworth, Pa. He graduated from M.I.T. and also studied cosmonautics in the Soviet Union through an exchange program with the Moscow Aviation Institute. He earned master’s degrees in aeronautics and astronautics from Stanford, and in planetary geology from the University of Houston-Clear Lake.

He is a retired U.S. Air Force colonel, who accumulated more than 2,000 flight hours in more than 30 types of aircraft.

“Mike approached every assignment with experience, humility and an unwavering focus on the mission,” said Scott Tingle, chief of the astronaut office at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. He added, “His legacy is woven into the way we fly today.”

As an astronaut, Mr. Fincke has often been credited for his leadership

When a machine that is designed to recycle astronauts’ sweat, urine and wastewater into drinking water malfunctioned aboard the station in November 2008, the astronauts then led by Mr. Fincke as mission commander spent nearly 54 hours conducting spacewalks that focused on repairing it.

(It was known as the “coffee machine” because, as one astronaut put it, “it’s going to take yesterday’s coffee and make it into today’s coffee.”)

When the arduous and intricate work was finally complete, Commander Fincke called down to mission control.

“Well, not to spoil anything,” he said, “but I think up here we’re feeling the appropriate words are ‘yippee!’”

item.title: South Carolina Senate Runoff Kicks Off With Chick-fil-A and Trump Calls
item.description:
The two-week runoff campaign to decide which Republican candidate will compete in November to succeed the late Senator Lindsey Graham started in the wee hours of Wednesday morning, as each candidate workshopped what their sales pitch should be.

Senator Darline Graham, Mr. Graham’s sister, had holed up at her campaign headquarters in Columbia, S.C., according to two people with knowledge of her night who requested anonymity to describe a private gathering. She discussed next steps on the phone with President Trump while she snacked on chicken nuggets and sweet tea from Chick-fil-A.

Representative Ralph Norman, the vice chairman of the House Freedom Caucus in his fifth term in Congress, was similarly ensconced on the other side of the state. His team released a television ad on Wednesday making the case that he is the only proven conservative in the race.

“You shouldn’t have to guess where your next senator stands,” he says in the ad. “With me, you already know.”

Ms. Graham and Mr. Norman emerged from a special election sprint on Tuesday to succeed Mr. Graham, who died unexpectedly in July. Now the two candidates are jumping into a two-week campaign for an Aug. 25 runoff that will be an even faster-paced foot race.

They defeated a wide field of other candidates in Tuesday’s primary, including Representative Russell Fry and former Gov. Mark Sanford. Ms. Graham is expected to make the case to voters who cast ballots for Mr. Fry, also a close ally of Mr. Trump, that they should choose her if they want a senator who is more aligned with the president. Mr. Sanford and Mr. Norman share a focus on fiscal conservatism.

Whoever emerges from the runoff will face Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee, though the seat is widely expected to stay in Republican hands in the deeply conservative state.

The contest between Ms. Graham and Mr. Norman is expected to center on their conservative credentials, along with Mr. Trump’s endorsement, in a state that voted for him by 18 points. Ms. Graham has already leveraged her status as the only Trump-backed candidate to undercut Mr. Norman, whom Trump may have spurned because he supported Nikki Haley for president in 2024. Mr. Norman has leaned on his hard-right voting record to present himself as the most dependable conservative in the field.

“This is one of the most important decisions that folks in our party have made in a generation,” Drew McKissick, chairman of the South Carolina Republican Party, said in an interview. “There are a lot of people whose preferred candidate didn’t make it last night, and so now we’re going to find out who their second choice was.”

Republican officials in the state have already started to pick sides. Senator Tim Scott, a Republican of South Carolina and chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, endorsed Ms. Graham on Wednesday. Mark Lynch, a businessman who ran in the special primary election, endorsed Mr. Norman.

Both candidates are entering the runoff with established political teams. Ms. Graham inherited the tenured political staff of her brother, who had won his primary for re-election before he died of an aortic tear. Mr. Norman ran in the Republican primary for governor in June. While he placed in third, the statewide campaign gave him the name recognition and organization to jump-start his campaign for Senate.

In the primary on Tuesday, he attracted strong support around the South Carolina suburbs of Charlotte, N.C., where he is from, and in the upstate region around Greenville, which is rich in Republican voters.

Ms. Graham, meanwhile, was largely unknown in the state until her brother’s death. While Mr. Trump’s endorsement did not prove to be enough to avoid a runoff on Tuesday, she over-performed expectations, particularly in the Midlands and along the northeast coast.

“The depth and breadth of her support across the state surprised some people,” said Rob Godfrey, a veteran Republican operative in South Carolina. “It’s going to be a test of whether she can run up margins in places along the coast and along the Grand Strand to offset the margins Ralph Norman will have in the upstate.”

On Tuesday night, Mr. Trump spoke multiple times with Ms. Graham over the phone. He lavished praise and offered her advice about next steps, said the two people familiar with her campaign.

“He was literally trying to help plan out the next two weeks,” one of the people said. “It was amazing.”

Ms. Graham has spent little time campaigning in the state, a choice she has blamed on her schedule as a newfound senator. Now that the chamber is in its August recess, she plans to spend the next two weeks talking to voters, she said on Tuesday morning after voting in Lexington, S.C.

On Wednesday night, less than a day after the final sprint began, Ms. Graham is scheduled to appear at her first runoff event: at a retirement community in Mr. Norman’s district.

item.title: Woman Arrested After Confessing to Starting Nevada Fire, Officials Say
item.description:
A woman was arrested after she told firefighters that she had intentionally set fires that became part of a larger blaze that is still burning along the border of California and Nevada, the authorities said Tuesday.

The woman, Christine Mitchell, 47, was arrested on suspicion of third-degree arson and possession of less than 14 grams of a controlled substance, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office in Nevada said in a statement on Tuesday. Ms. Mitchell’s public defender didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Mitchell left a home near Freds Mountain Road and set multiple fires, the sheriff’s office said. She caught the attention of firefighters who were responding to the resulting blaze, known as the Fred Mountain fire, and told them she had meant to start the fire.

The Fred Mountain fire, which is burning north of Reno, Nev., has since merged with another nearby wildfire, known as the Bug fire. The Bug fire has covered more than 70,000 acres and has forced thousands of people to evacuate, including from tribal land. It’s one of many large wildfires burning in the western United States during a fire season that has been unusually active for much of the region.

Ms. Mitchell was taken into custody on Sunday. Senior Judge Derek Dreiling at the Reno Justice Court set her bail at $80,000 on Tuesday, according to court records.

The sheriff’s office did not explain what the authorities believed Ms. Mitchell’s motive might have been for starting the fires.

The Reno-Sparks Indian Colony declared an emergency in response to the fires, and its Hungry Valley community was evacuated. Another large blaze east of the Bug fire, called the Stallion fire, is threatening Pyramid Lake Paiute tribal land. The Stallion fire, which officials said was caused by a human, was not contained as of Wednesday morning.

“We understand our Hungry Valley residents are frustrated,” Bethany Sam, a spokeswoman for Reno-Sparks Indian Colony, said during a Facebook livestream Tuesday night. “We know you all want to come home, check on your property, take care of your animals and get back to your normal lives.”

Gov. Joe Lombardo of Nevada also declared a state of emergency on Monday, citing a shortage of wildland fire resources as several wildfires burned across the region.

This week, the Federal Emergency Management Agency authorized the use of federal funds to help Nevada fight the fires.

item.title: Hegseth Says Anti-Cartel Coalition Will Do ‘Bad Things to Bad People’
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called on military leaders in Latin America on Wednesday to ramp up their fight against drug traffickers and join the U.S. military in operations against cartels.

Mr. Hegseth, speaking to civilian defense leaders and top generals from 18 other countries at a meeting of a U.S.-led counter-cartel coalition in Panama, doubled down on the Trump administration’s pledge to use military force in addition to law enforcement measures to combat drug traffickers.

The collective goal is “to degrade, dismantle and destroy narco-terrorist networks,” said Mr. Hegseth, speaking on the sidelines of a major U.S.-led regional training exercise in Panama.

With his typical bravado, Mr. Hegseth said the cartel-busting coalition’s motto would be, “We do bad things to bad people.”

The Trump administration has in recent months stepped up its cooperation with allies across Latin America to combat the drug trade. It created the coalition, part of the regional Shield of the Americas alliance, and convened its first meeting in March.

That month, Ecuador and the United States launched joint military operations against designated terrorist groups. In May, the Pentagon pressed Guatemala to agree to joint U.S. airstrikes and other military action inside its borders to target suspected drug groups.

Mr. Hegseth said on Wednesday that Honduras and Colombia had also agreed to allow joint operations.

Last week, the military’s U.S. Southern Command announced Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, setting up the infrastructure for an expansion of its war against drugs in cooperation with regional allies.

This new task force builds on a yearlong Pentagon campaign in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, where the military has conducted 66 boat strikes that have killed at least 221 people who it says, without presenting evidence, were trafficking drugs.

Legal experts have warned that the strikes are illegal, because the military cannot deliberately target civilians who are not directly participating in hostilities, even if they are breaking the law. Trafficking drugs, they say, does not rise to the standard of hostilities.

On Wednesday, Mr. Hegseth asserted that these strikes have decreased the number of suspected drug vessels by more than half in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. But a recent investigation by The New York Times revealed that cocaine, by far the top drug smuggled out of South America, is as easy to get in much of the United States as it was before the strikes began.

The United States also recently announced it was fast-tracking military cooperation with Colombia, where voters elected a right-wing president in June. The country could emerge as a key piece of the U.S. push against traffickers and organized crime in the region.

Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine and has in the past been a staunch U.S. ally.

For the last four years, however, relations between the two countries grew strained as Colombia’s leftist former president, Gustavo Petro, spoke out frequently against President Trump’s boat strikes and other policies toward the region.

For decades, U.S. policy in Latin America has centered on counternarcotics. Billions have been spent on military assistance, crop eradication and more; leaders have pressed for hard-line security measures and extradition agreements.

In his second term, Mr. Trump has gone further, treating drug traffickers not as criminals but as enemy combatants.

Blaming cartels and drug gangs for America’s overdose crisis and for fueling violent crime, the Trump administration has added around 20 groups to its list of foreign terrorist organizations since 2025 — from major Mexican cartels to Ecuadorean drug gangs — and has authorized using lethal force against them.

Last year, Mr. Trump justified the military’s strikes on small boats by claiming that the United States was engaged in a formal “armed conflict” with traffickers that had been designated as terrorist organizations, and that smugglers for such groups were “unlawful combatants.”

The military’s most recent strike, which killed eight people, was on June 21. Pentagon officials say there has been a pause since then partly because military teams and equipment were diverted to help provide humanitarian relief to victims of the recent earthquake in Venezuela.

Now the Trump administration appears to be moving its efforts targeting armed groups in Latin America from international waters onto land.

To date, 18 countries have joined the Pentagon-led counter-cartel coalition: Argentina, the Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago.

The head of Southern Command, Gen. Francis Donovan, said in an online post on Aug. 3 that the coalition’s new task force would “take the fight to the enemy.”

Mr. Hegseth met with officials in Panama City during a visit in April 2025 and signed a bilateral security agreement with Panama’s president, José Raúl Mulino, a conservative who has been eager to negotiate with the Trump administration after facing threats over the Panama Canal. Panama does not have an active military.

Nations that do not officially have agreements with the United States have nevertheless been the sites of highly publicized operations since Mr. Trump took office last year.

Mr. Trump applauded a C.I.A.-involved strike early this year in Mexico that helped kill Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, one of the world’s most powerful drug trafficking organizations.

Mr. Trump also celebrated a strike in Venezuela that killed a leader of Tren de Aragua, a transnational group that he says has invaded the United States and perpetrated murders and other violence.

Experts say that organized crime and trafficking have expanded across the region in places where the government is absent and that illicit activities have spiked since the pandemic.

They caution, however, that past U.S.-led “drug wars” in the region have failed to curb the drug trade — and note that today, much of South America’s cocaine heads to Europe, not the United States.

Human rights groups also warn that militarizing the fight against armed groups risks increasing violence that threatens civilians.

Notably absent from the regional anti-trafficking alliance — and the conference in Panama this week — is Mexico, home to formidable cartels that traffic fentanyl and other deadly drugs into the United States. Like Brazil, which is not in the regional alliance either, Mexico is led by a left-wing leader, Claudia Sheinbaum.

Wary of the public backlash in a country with a long history of U.S. military intervention, and determined to protect Mexican sovereignty, Ms. Sheinbaum has stuck to a simple message: “Coordination but not subordination.”

item.title: ICE Agent Who Pushed Activist to the Ground Pleads Guilty
item.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor battery charge on Wednesday for throwing an activist to the ground near Chicago last year during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the region.

A judge in Cook County, Ill., sentenced the agent, Adam Saracco, to 12 months of supervision on Wednesday and ordered him not to have contact with the activist he had clashed with, Robert Held.

Mr. Saracco, 41, was charged with misdemeanor battery earlier this year after the altercation in December. At a gas station in Brookfield, Ill., Mr. Held was filming Mr. Saracco when Mr. Saracco approached him. Mr. Saracco took Mr. Held’s phone and threw him to the ground. Mr. Saracco was off duty at the time and was getting gas after leaving a nearby immigration detention center. Mr. Held said he did not sustain any injuries.

It was not clear whether Mr. Saracco was still employed by ICE. Neither Mr. Saracco nor the Department of Homeland Security responded to requests for comment on Wednesday.

Mr. Held, a trust and estate lawyer, joined many Illinois residents in protesting against ICE last fall amid a surge in immigration arrests across the Chicago area, which the Trump administration called Operation Midway Blitz.

“I am pleased that there is some accountability,” Mr. Held, 68, said in an interview on Wednesday. He added that he remained “deeply troubled and concerned” by the actions of federal agents.

“This resolution represents an important step for accountability and shows that Cook County will not turn a blind eye to unlawful conduct, no matter who you are,” Eileen O’Neill Burke, the state’s attorney for Cook County, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Ms. Burke said that her office would seek justice on behalf of those harmed during the Trump administration’s crackdown in the Chicago area “when the evidence and the law allow us to prosecute.” There have been very few local prosecutions of immigration agents.

item.title: A Fight Over Abortion and Surrogacy Ends With a Baby Born in Texas
item.description:
A bitter confrontation over surrogacy, abortion and parental rights that stretched across three states culminated on Wednesday with the birth of the baby at the center of the conflict at a Dallas hospital.

The fate of the baby, who has a severe birth defect, became a cause this summer among anti-abortion activists, who provided legal representation for the surrogate, McKenna West, and helped her travel to Texas for medical care. This week, she also received support from the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, who took legal action to compel medical treatments for the newborn.

The dispute began in the spring after the discovery at around 20 weeks of pregnancy that the fetus had a rare and life-threatening congenital heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and would require multiple surgeries to survive.

The intended parents, who live in Los Angeles, opted to terminate the pregnancy.

But Ms. West, who lives in Alaska, refused to have an abortion. Instead, she went to Texas, which bans abortion, to seek specialists who could treat the baby’s defect.

On Wednesday, amid overlapping legal actions in the three states, Ms. West gave birth to a boy in Dallas whom activists have called “Baby Gabriel.” His legal parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, chose a different name.

“As if the heartbreak of his condition were not enough, they are devastated to see their family tragedy transformed into political theater by the Texas Attorney General’s office and McKenna West,” said a lawyer for the parents, Lee Budner, in a statement.

Mr. Budner said the boy was “now receiving medical care provided by a team of pediatric experts,” adding that the parents “would place their baby’s health and well-being first, following the advice of the baby’s medical team.”

Ms. West is seeking custody of the child.

The birth came just days after Mr. Paxton’s legal intervention on Monday. Mr. Paxton, a Republican locked in a tough race for the U.S. Senate, argued in Dallas County court that the parents were required to provide lifesaving care under Texas law.

“My office will use every tool available to protect innocent lives,” Mr. Paxton said in a statement.

The move sharply increased attention on what had already been a cause célèbre in anti-abortion circles this summer.

By Tuesday, Mr. Paxton celebrated having secured a temporary restraining order, or T.R.O., in Dallas that prevents the parents from removing the child from Texas until a hearing in late August. The order also requires them to provide “medically indicated, lifesaving treatment” to the baby.

At the same time, the Dallas County court also issued another restraining order against Ms. West. The order bars Ms. West from presenting herself as the baby’s parent, guardian or medical-decision maker “to anyone.”

“Unfortunately, because of the Texas T.R.O. that was entered yesterday, McKenna didn’t get to see or hold him after he was born,” Lincoln Wilson, a lawyer for Ms. West, said in an interview.

Ms. West, who did not respond to an interview request for this story, said in an interview this month with the former Fox News and current YouTube host Megyn Kelly that she did not support abortion and felt “trapped” by the surrogacy contract, which permitted the intended parents to end the pregnancy via abortion.

“It brought up a lot of fear,” said Ms. West, a nurse with two children of her own, in the interview.

Through a mutual friend, Ms. West connected with Lila Rose, the president of Live Action, an anti-abortion group. Ms. Rose said she helped Ms. West get legal support from the Alliance Defending Freedom, a prominent Christian conservative legal organization.

“There came a point where she, for the sake of her own medical care and safety, needed to travel to Texas, and so we did assist,” Ms. Rose said. “They were treating her baby like a product. The product had a defect, and so they were trying to send it back.”

Ms. Rose said that her organization does not support surrogacy, which “commoditizes human life” and leads to “heartbreaking and devastating situations like this.”

Mr. Wilson, the lawyer for Ms. West, said that the legal case was not over and that Ms. West would continue to fight for custody of the boy, who must undergo weeks of surgeries “before he’s really in the clear.”

item.title: The Debate Over Democrats’ Future Rages On After Hong’s Defeat in Wisconsin
item.description:
Francesca Hong was supposed to prove that a democratic socialist could win a statewide election.

Instead, her surprise loss in the primary election for governor of Wisconsin dealt a blow to the progressive movement and initiated a scramble among Democratic factions to define her narrow defeat either as an impressive harbinger of the movement’s future or an ominous sign of voter antipathy toward the far left.

Some prominent Democrats argued that the outcome was proof that the moderate wing of the party carried more electoral weight than the progressive one, which has dominated headlines this year as insurgent candidates have ousted incumbents in deep-blue cities.

Others, on the left, looked to celebrate the tight race — even though their candidate fell short — as evidence that progressives can compete in statewide contests.

“It’s a significant loss,” Robert Lasica, a spokesman for Madison’s Democratic Socialists of America chapter, said in an interview. But he argued the race was also “a big triumph of how far we can go with building the left infrastructure in Wisconsin that simply did not exist a year ago.”

David Crowley, who is the Milwaukee County executive and had briefly suspended his campaign just over a month ago, defeated Ms. Hong by a razor-thin margin. His victory defied months of polls that showed Ms. Hong far in the lead.

It was the second consecutive week with a Democratic primary in which a progressive candidate underperformed expectations. Last week in the Democratic Senate race in Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens, but the contest was closer than expected and was not called until the next morning. Both narrow outcomes have kept the debate that has been raging all year between moderates and progressives vigorously alive.

Mr. El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and the D.S.A. is not officially part of the Democratic Party. But both the D.S.A. and non-D.S.A. progressives have roiled the party in this year’s midterms by exciting the left flank of the party’s base.

Some in the party hoped to export aspects of Ms. Hong’s success to other campaigns, notably her ground game. The former chef and restaurateur spent more time than any other candidate campaigning in rural Wisconsin, and it appeared to pay off with strong margins in some of those counties. Progressives have won a string of races partly on the strength of their ground games. The question is whether the model can be replicated without the populist policy proposals, such as abolishing I.C.E., that are resonating with some voters but that many moderates eschew.

The fallout of Ms. Hong’s campaign carries extra weight as the party eyes 2028, with those in each wing already jockeying to elevate their own. On Wednesday, Democrats openly exploring presidential bids sought to wield the election results to make their cases.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and former chief of staff to President Barack Obama, wrote on social media that Ms. Hong’s defeat showed “that the pragmatic wing isn’t a faction of this party. It’s the majority, it’s awake now, and it’s exerting itself.”

Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive congressman from California who had endorsed Ms. Hong and is also contemplating a run for president, sought to tamp down criticism of the far left.

“I appreciate that Democrats can have differences over single payer healthcare, free childcare, pausing data centers and other issues @FrancescaHongWI fought for,” he wrote on X. “But caricaturing and labeling candidates based on a few statements is not a politics I believe in.”

Democratic socialists had seen Wisconsin as a key opportunity to prove that their message could resonate in less liberal parts of the country. While they planned to study Ms. Hong’s loss to improve their electoral fortunes, several said they viewed Tuesday’s result as strong proof of the movement’s rise.

“Francesa won hundreds of thousands of votes — one of the highest vote totals of a democratic socialist candidate in any election in the United States,” said Katie Sims, a D.S.A. member in Ithaca, N.Y., who leads the group’s national electoral strategy. “Ultimately, it’s disappointing that she lost by such a small margin, but really heartening that it shows that these kinds of races are viable.”

D.S.A. members pointed to several areas for improvement. For one, the socialist infrastructure and campaign experience in Wisconsin was far less robust than in places such as New York City, which last fall elected Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, to be mayor. There, socialists had been building for years toward that victory as well as additional successes in congressional campaigns in June.

“For some people on the campaign, they have not worked at this scale yet before under these pressures,” Mr. Lasica said. “Next time around, we’re going to be in a better position.”

Some progressives criticized some of the biggest national names in their movement, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, for sitting out the race.

Ms. Hong also struggled in the final days of her campaign to explain past online remarks that were unearthed in news reports — including one in which she suggested canceling Thanksgiving.

Those reports unfurled an examination on the left, too, of how positions and rhetoric of pandemic-era progressivism have not always aged well with the broader population. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez jumped into that debate on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, describing that era as “crazy” and “Woke 1.0” — a term that has become a political meme.

Asked about those comments on Wednesday and whether “Woke 1.0” was indeed crazy, Mr. Mamdani stressed that elected officials have a responsibility to own their evolving beliefs.

“I think that each person has a responsibility to tell New Yorkers, to tell Americans, when they’re running for office what they believe,” he said to reporters. “And sometimes what you believe can change, it can develop, it can grow.”

Dana Rubinstein and Tim Balk contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Federal Hate Crime Charge Filed in Stabbing of Muslim Man in Utah
item.description:
A man in Utah was indicted on a federal hate crime charge after he rode a scooter to a mall, bought a knife and repeatedly stabbed a Muslim man selling wares at a kiosk, the authorities said on Wednesday.

Federal prosecutors in Salt Lake City said Peter Larsen, 48, was indicted in connection with a stabbing on July 13 at the mall, in West Valley City. The victim was stabbed about a dozen times, on his head, chest and arms, causing internal bleeding, the authorities said, and a man who tried to intervene was also stabbed.

Mr. Larsen also faced state charges, including two counts of attempted aggravated murder and one count of having a dangerous weapon, according to the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office. It was not immediately clear what would happen with the state charges as the federal case proceeded.

“An alleged unprovoked attack on anyone in our community is unacceptable, but an attack allegedly motivated because of the victim’s religion is alarming,” the Salt Lake County district attorney, Sim Gill, said in a statement announcing the state charges.

Mr. Gill did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was not clear whether Mr. Larsen had a lawyer. Mr. Larsen faces life in prison on the federal count, according to U.S. prosecutors.

The attack began when Mr. Larsen approached the victim and asked for water, according to a charging document filed by the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office. The authorities have said the ordeal was captured on the mall’s surveillance video and on witnesses’ cellphones.

Mr. Larsen asked the victim if he was Muslim, and after hearing that he was, Mr. Larsen said, “Everything is like Jesus Christ,” prosecutors said. He then began stabbing the man with a knife he had bought earlier that day, they said.

Several witnesses rushed toward Mr. Larsen and tried to subdue him. One person punched Mr. Larsen repeatedly, knocking him out, prosecutors said.

Another witness said he heard the victim calling for God and his mother.

Mr. Larsen told the authorities that he had planned to arrive at the mall and make an “exhibition of Muslims and hopefully be a catalyst so people would rid the country of Muslims,” prosecutors said.

Mr. Larsen also may have communicated with other people who shared his anti-Muslim beliefs, his brother told the authorities, according to prosecutors.

Witnesses told the authorities that Mr. Larsen approached other brown-skinned people in the mall and questioned their ethnicity and religious beliefs. The individuals who identified as Muslim worked behind a counter, rendering them inaccessible to Mr. Larsen, prosecutors said.

“Unfortunately for victim, he was working at a kiosk completely exposed and accessible,” they said.

Mr. Larsen will appear in court on Thursday in Salt Lake City. He has previous convictions of assaulting a police officer, arson and driving under the influence, prosecutors said.
